1 In nova fert animus mutatas dicere formas
2 corpora; di, coeptis (nam vos mutastis et illas)
3 adspirate meis primaque ab origine mundi
4 ad mea perpetuum deducite tempora carmen.
5 Ante mare et terras et quod tegit omnia caelum
6 unus erat toto naturae vultus in orbe,
7 quem dixere chaos: rudis indigestaque moles
8 nec quicquam nisi pondus iners congestaque eodem
9 non bene iunctarum discordia semina rerum.
10 nullus adhuc mundo praebebat lumina Titan,
11 nec nova crescendo reparabat cornua Phoebe,
12 nec circumfuso pendebat in aere tellus
13 ponderibus librata suis, nec bracchia longo
14 margine terrarum porrexerat Amphitrite;
15 utque aer, tellus illic et pontus et aether.
16 Sic erat instabilis tellus, innabilis unda,
17 lucis egens aer: nulli sua forma manebat,
18 obstabatque aliis aliud, quia corpore in uno
19 frigida pugnabant calidis, umentia siccis,
20 mollia cum duris, sine pondere habentia pondus.
21 Hanc deus et melior litem natura diremit.
22 Nam caelo terras et terris abscidit undas,
23 et liquidum spisso secrevit ab aere caelum.
24 Quae postquam evolvit caecoque exemit acervo,
25 dissociata locis concordi pace ligavit.
26 Ignea convexi vis et sine pondere caeli
27 emicuit summaque locum sibi fecit in arce:
28 proximus est aer illi levitate locoque:
29 densior his tellus, elementaque grandia traxit
30 et pressa est gravitate sua: circumfluus umor

1 My soul is wrought to sing of forms transformed 2 to bodies new and strange! Immortal Gods 3 inspire my heart, for ye have changed yourselves 4 and all things you have changed! Oh lead my song 5 in smooth and measured strains, from olden days 6 when earth began to this completed time!

52 Inminet his aer. Qui quanto est pondere terrae,
53 pondere aquae levior tanto est onerosior igni.
54 Illic et nebulas, illic consistere nubes
55 iussit et humanas motura tonitrua mentes
56 et cum fulminibus facientes fulgura ventos.
57 His quoque non passim mundi fabricator habendum
58 aera permisit: vix nunc obsistitur illis,
59 cum sua quisque regant diverso flamina tractu,
60 quin lanient mundum: tanta est discordia fratrum.

7 Before the ocean and the earth appeared— 8 before the skies had overspread them all— 9 the face of Nature in a vast expanse 10 was naught but Chaos uniformly waste. 11 It was a rude and undeveloped mass, 12 that nothing made except a ponderous weight; 13 and all discordant elements confused, 14 were there congested in a shapeless heap. 15 As yet the sun afforded earth no light, 16 nor did the moon renew her crescent horns; 17 the earth was not suspended in the air 18 exactly balanced by her heavy weight. 19 Not far along the margin of the shores 20 had Amphitrite stretched her lengthened arms,— 21 for all the land was mixed with sea and air. 22 The land was soft, the sea unfit to sail, 23 the atmosphere opaque, to naught was given 24 a proper form, in everything was strife, 25 and all was mingled in a seething mass— 26 with hot the cold parts strove, and wet with dry 27 and soft with hard, and weight with empty void. 28 But God, or kindly Nature, ended strife— 29 he cut the land from skies, the sea from land, 30 the heavens ethereal from material air; 31 and when were all evolved from that dark mass 32 he bound the fractious parts in tranquil peace. 33 The fiery element of convex heaven 34 leaped from the mass devoid of dragging weight, 35 and chose the summit arch to which the air 36 as next in quality was next in place. 37 The earth more dense attracted grosser parts 38 and moved by gravity sank underneath; 39 and last of all the wide surrounding waves 40 in deeper channels rolled around the globe. 41 And when this God —which one is yet unknown— 42 had carved asunder that discordant mass, 43 had thus reduced it to its elements, 44 that every part should equally combine, 45 when time began He rounded out the earth 46 and moulded it to form a mighty globe. 47 Then poured He forth the deeps and gave command 48 that they should billow in the rapid winds, 49 that they should compass every shore of earth. 50 he also added fountains, pools and lakes, 51 and bound with shelving banks the slanting streams, 52 which partly are absorbed and partly join 53 the boundless ocean. Thus received amid 54 the wide expanse of uncontrolled waves, 55 they beat the shores instead of crooked banks. 56 At His command the boundless plains extend, 57 the valleys are depressed, the woods are clothed 58 in green, the stony mountains rise. And as 59 the heavens are intersected on the right 60 by two broad zones, by two that cut the left, 61 and by a fifth consumed with ardent heat, 62 with such a number did the careful God 63 mark off the compassed weight, and thus the earth 64 received as many climes.—Such heat consumes 65 the middle zone that none may dwell therein; 66 and two extremes are covered with deep snow;

67 and two are placed betwixt the hot and cold, 68 which mixed together give a temperate clime; 69 and over all the atmosphere suspends 70 with weight proportioned to the fiery sky, 71 exactly as the weight of earth compares 72 with weight of water. 73 And He ordered mist 74 to gather in the air and spread the clouds. 75 He fixed the thunders that disturb our souls, 76 and brought the lightning on destructive winds 77 that also waft the cold. Nor did the great 78 Artificer permit these mighty winds 79 to blow unbounded in the pathless skies, 80 but each discordant brother fixed in space, 81 although His power can scarce restrain their rage 82 to rend the universe. At His command 83 to far Aurora, Eurus took his way, 84 to Nabath, Persia, and that mountain range 85 first gilded by the dawn; and Zephyr's flight 86 was towards the evening star and peaceful shores, 87 warm with the setting sun; and Boreas 88 invaded Scythia and the northern snows; 89 and Auster wafted to the distant south 90 where clouds and rain encompass his abode.— 91 and over these He fixed the liquid sky, 92 devoid of weight and free from earthly dross. 93 And scarcely had He separated these 94 and fixed their certain bounds, when all the stars, 95 which long were pressed and hidden in the mass, 96 began to gleam out from the plains of heaven,

103 contentique cibis nullo cogente creatis

113 Postquam, Saturno tenebrosa in Tartara misso,

97 and traversed, with the Gods, bright ether fields: 98 and lest some part might be bereft of life 99 the gleaming waves were filled with twinkling fish; 100 the earth was covered with wild animals; 101 the agitated air was filled with birds. 102 But one more perfect and more sanctified, 103 a being capable of lofty thought, 104 intelligent to rule, was wanting still 105 man was created! Did the Unknown God 106 designing then a better world make man 107 of seed divine? or did Prometheus 108 take the new soil of earth (that still contained 109 some godly element of Heaven's Life) 110 and use it to create the race of man; 111 first mingling it with water of new streams; 112 so that his new creation, upright man, 113 was made in image of commanding Gods? 114 On earth the brute creation bends its gaze, 115 but man was given a lofty countenance 116 and was commanded to behold the skies; 117 and with an upright face may view the stars:— 118 and so it was that shapeless clay put on 119 the form of man till then unknown to earth. 120 First was the Golden Age. Then rectitude 121 spontaneous in the heart prevailed, and faith. 122 Avengers were not seen, for laws unframed 123 were all unknown and needless. Punishment 124 and fear of penalties existed not. 125 No harsh decrees were fixed on brazen plates. 126 No suppliant multitude the countenance 127 of Justice feared, averting, for they dwelt 128 without a judge in peace. Descended not 129 the steeps, shorn from its height, the lofty pine, 130 cleaving the trackless waves of alien shores, 131 nor distant realms were known to wandering men. 132 The towns were not entrenched for time of war; 133 they had no brazen trumpets, straight, nor horns 134 of curving brass, nor helmets, shields nor swords. 135 There was no thought of martial pomp —secure 136 a happy multitude enjoyed repose. 137 Then of her own accord the earth produced 138 a store of every fruit. The harrow touched 139 her not, nor did the plowshare wound 140 her fields. And man content with given food, 141 and none compelling, gathered arbute fruits 142 and wild strawberries on the mountain sides, 143 and ripe blackberries clinging to the bush, 144 and corners and sweet acorns on the ground, 145 down fallen from the spreading tree of Jove. 146 Eternal Spring! Soft breathing zephyrs soothed 147 and warmly cherished buds and blooms, produced 148 without a seed. The valleys though unplowed 149 gave many fruits; the fields though not renewed

150 white glistened with the heavy bearded wheat: 151 rivers flowed milk and nectar, and the trees, 152 the very oak trees, then gave honey of themselves. 153 When Saturn had been banished into night 154 and all the world was ruled by Jove supreme, 155 the Silver Age, though not so good as gold 156 but still surpassing yellow brass, prevailed. 157 Jove first reduced to years the Primal Spring, 158 by him divided into periods four, 159 unequal,—summer, autumn, winter, spring.— 160 then glowed with tawny heat the parched air, 161 or pendent icicles in winter froze 162 and man stopped crouching in crude caverns, while 163 he built his homes of tree rods, bark entwined. 164 Then were the cereals planted in long rows, 165 and bullocks groaned beneath the heavy yoke. 166 The third Age followed, called The Age of Bronze, 167 when cruel people were inclined to arms 168 but not to impious crimes. And last of all 169 the ruthless and hard Age of Iron prevailed, 170 from which malignant vein great evil sprung; 171 and modesty and faith and truth took flight, 172 and in their stead deceits and snares and frauds 173 and violence and wicked love of gain, 174 succeeded.—Then the sailor spread his sails 175 to winds unknown, and keels that long had stood 176 on lofty mountains pierced uncharted waves. 177 Surveyors anxious marked with metes and bounds 178 the lands, created free as light and air: 179 nor need the rich ground furnish only crops,

180 and give due nourishment by right required,— 181 they penetrated to the bowels of earth 182 and dug up wealth, bad cause of all our ills,— 183 rich ores which long ago the earth had hid 184 and deep removed to gloomy Stygian caves: 185 and soon destructive iron and harmful gold 186 were brought to light; and War, which uses both, 187 came forth and shook with sanguinary grip 188 his clashing arms. Rapacity broke forth— 189 the guest was not protected from his host, 190 the father in law from his own son in law; 191 even brothers seldom could abide in peace. 192 The husband threatened to destroy his wife, 193 and she her husband: horrid step dames mixed 194 the deadly henbane: eager sons inquired 195 their fathers, ages. Piety was slain: 196 and last of all the virgin deity, 197 Astraea vanished from the blood-stained earth. 198 And lest ethereal heights should long remain 199 less troubled than the earth, the throne of Heaven 200 was threatened by the Giants; and they piled 201 mountain on mountain to the lofty stars. 202 But Jove, omnipotent, shot thunderbolts 203 through Mount Olympus, and he overturned 204 from Ossa huge, enormous Pelion. 205 And while these dreadful bodies lay overwhelmed 206 in their tremendous bulk, (so fame reports) 207 the Earth was reeking with the copious blood 208 of her gigantic sons; and thus replete 209 with moisture she infused the steaming gore

216 When, from his throne 217 supreme, the Son of Saturn viewed their deeds, 218 he deeply groaned: and calling to his mind 219 the loathsome feast Lycaon had prepared, 220 a recent deed not common to report, 221 his soul conceived great anger —worthy Jove— 222 and he convened a council. No delay 223 detained the chosen Gods. 224 When skies are clear 225 a path is well defined on high, which men, 226 because so white, have named the Milky Way. 227 It makes a passage for the deities 228 and leads to mansions of the Thunder God, 229 to Jove's imperial home. On either side 230 of its wide way the noble Gods are seen, 231 inferior Gods in other parts abide, 232 but there the potent and renowned of Heaven 233 have fixed their homes.—It is a glorious place, 234 our most audacious verse might designate 235 the “Palace of High Heaven.” When the Gods 236 were seated, therefore, in its marble halls 237 the King of all above the throng sat high, 238 and leaning on his ivory scepter, thrice, 239 and once again he shook his awful locks, 240 wherewith he moved the earth, and seas and stars,— 241 and thus indignantly began to speak; 242 “The time when serpent footed giants strove 243 to fix their hundred arms on captive Heaven, 244 not more than this event could cause alarm 245 for my dominion of the universe.

246 Although it was a savage enemy, 247 yet warred we with a single source derived 248 of one. Now must I utterly destroy 249 this mortal race wherever Nereus roars 250 around the world. Yea, by the Infernal Streams 251 that glide through Stygian groves beneath the world, 252 I swear it. Every method has been tried. 253 The knife must cut immedicable wounds, 254 lest maladies infect untainted parts. 255 “Beneath my sway are demi gods and fauns, 256 nymphs, rustic deities, sylvans of the hills, 257 satyrs;—all these, unworthy Heaven's abodes, 258 we should at least permit to dwell on earth 259 which we to them bequeathed. What think ye, Gods, 260 is safety theirs when I, your sovereign lord, 261 the Thunder-bolt Controller, am ensnared 262 by fierce Lycaon?” Ardent in their wrath, 263 the astonished Gods demand revenge overtake 264 this miscreant; he who dared commit such crimes. 265 'Twas even thus when raged that impious band 266 to blot the Roman name in sacred blood 267 of Caesar, sudden apprehensive fears 268 of ruin absolute astonished man, 269 and all the world convulsed. Nor is the love 270 thy people bear to thee, Augustus, less 271 than these displayed to Jupiter whose voice 272 and gesture all the murmuring host restrained: 273 and as indignant clamour ceased, suppressed 274 by regnant majesty, Jove once again 275 broke the deep silence with imperial words;
